Chapter Two: The First Lessons—Learning About Money Outside the Classroom.
Picture this—it's just an ordinary Saturday morning. Two boys, feeling frustrated because they don’t have any spending money, decide they're going to do something about it. So, what do they do? They collect empty toothpaste tubes from their neighbors, melt them down, and try to make their own coins.
It doesn’t take long for an adult to step in and let them know—hey, you can't just make your own money, that's illegal! But here’s the thing: instead of shutting them down, the friend’s dad sees a teachable moment.
He invites the boys to work at his store, offering them a little bit of pay for dusting cans and stocking shelves. The work? Honestly, it’s boring. And the pay feels... well, not worth the effort. After a few weeks, the boys are ready to give up, thinking—shouldn’t working hard mean you get rewarded?
But the store owner doesn’t coddle them. Instead, he offers a challenge: “Most people spend their lives working for money, never realizing they could make money work for them.”
At first, the boys don’t really get it. But as they keep showing up at the store, they start to notice things. Customers rush in and out, spending money without much thought. Employees repeat the same tasks every day, heads down. But the business owner? He isn’t stuck behind the counter. He’s always looking for ways to grow his business, thinking bigger.
Then, one afternoon, something clicks. The boys realize that all the comic books people read are just being tossed out. So, they ask the owner—can we collect those comics? With a little bit of negotiation, they get permission. Next thing you know, they set up a comic book reading room in the basement, charging the neighborhood kids a few cents to come in and read.
It’s not glamorous, but suddenly, they’re making money—without having to be there every second. This is the first time they really see what it means to create something that earns for you, even when you’re not working.
That experience sticks with them. Most of us are taught that you’ve got to trade your time for money—that working harder is the only way to get ahead. But these boys learn something different. They see that if you’re creative, observant, and willing to do what others don’t, new opportunities start to show up.
At home, though, things sound different. One parent keeps pushing the idea of playing it safe, aiming for job security and a steady paycheck. Meanwhile, the store owner is all about taking risks and learning by doing. And that’s when the boys realize—real financial education doesn’t usually happen in a classroom. It comes from rolling up your sleeves, trying things out, sometimes failing, and always asking the questions that everyone else is afraid to ask.
